'''Project Euler''' (named after [[Leonhard Euler]]) is a [[website]] dedicated to a series of [[computational problem]]s intended to be solved with [[computer program]]s.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2015/10/12/opinion/the-importance-of-recreational-math.html| title=The importance of recreational math |last=Suri |first=Manil |date=12 October 2015 |access-date=5 June 2018 |newspaper=[[The New York Times]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|title=Learning to Program|series=Addison-Wesley learning series|first=Steven|last=Foote|publisher=Pearson Education|year=2014|isbn=9780789753397|page=249|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=m4IhBQAAQBAJ&pg=PA249}}</ref> The project attracts graduates and students interested in [[mathematics]] and [[computer programming]].  Since its creation in 2001 by Colin Hughes, Project Euler has gained notability and popularity worldwide.<ref>{{cite news
 | url=https://www.theatlantic.com/technology/print/2011/06/how-i-failed-failed-and-finally-succeeded-at-learning-how-to-code/239855/
 | title=How I Failed, Failed, and Finally Succeeded at Learning How to Code - Technology
 | work=The Atlantic
 | author=James Somers
 | date=June 2011
 | accessdate=14 December 2013 }}
</ref> It includes 1007 problems {{as of|2026|07|lc=y}},<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://projecteuler.net/recent|title=Recent Problems - Project Euler|access-date=9 May 2025}}</ref> with a new one added approximately every week.<ref>{{Cite web|title=News - Project Euler|url=https://projecteuler.net/news|access-date=27 April 2021|website=projecteuler.net}}</ref> Problems are of varying difficulty, but each is solvable in less than a minute of [[CPU time]] using an efficient algorithm on a modestly powered computer.<ref name="about">{{cite web|url=https://projecteuler.net/about |title=About - Project Euler |access-date=23 March 2023}}</ref>

==Features of the site==
A forum specific to each question may be viewed after the user has correctly answered the given question.<ref name="about" /> Problems can be sorted on ID, number solved and difficulty. Participants can track their progress through achievement levels based on the number of problems solved. A new level is reached for every 25 problems solved. Special awards exist for solving special combinations of problems. For instance, there is an award for solving fifty prime numbered problems. A special "Eulerians" level exists to track achievement based on the fastest fifty solvers of recent problems so that newer members can compete without solving older problems.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://projecteuler.net/news_archives |title=Project Euler (News Archives) |accessdate = 31 March 2015}}</ref>

== Example problem and solutions ==
The first Project Euler problem is '''[https://projecteuler.net/problem=1 Multiples of 3 and 5]'''
<blockquote>If we list all the natural numbers below 10 that are multiples of 3 or 5, we get 3, 5, 6 and 9. The sum of these multiples is 23.

Find the sum of all the multiples of 3 or 5 below 1000.
</blockquote>

It is a difficulty level 0 problem, indicating it is one of the easiest on the site. The initial approach a beginner can come up with is a [[Brute-force search|bruteforce]] attempt. Given the upper bound of 1000 in this case, a bruteforce is easily achievable for most current home computers. A Python code that solves it is presented below.
<syntaxhighlight lang="python3">
def solve(limit: int) -> int:
    total = 0
    for i in range(limit):
        if i % 3 == 0 or i % 5 == 0:
            total += i
    return total

print(solve(1000))
</syntaxhighlight>
This solution has a [[Big O notation|Big ''O'' notation]] of <math>O(n)</math>. A user could keep refining their solution for any given problem further. In this case, there exists a constant time solution for the problem.

The [[inclusion-exclusion principle]] claims that if there are two finite sets <math>A, B</math>, the number of elements in their union can be expressed as <math>|A \cup B| = |A| + |B| - |A \cap B|</math>. This is a pretty popular combinatorics result. One can extend this result and express a relation for the sum of their elements, namely

<math>\sum_{x \in A \cup B} x = \sum_{x \in A} x + \sum_{x \in B} x - \sum_{x \in A \cap B} x </math>

Applying this to the problem, have <math>A </math> denote the multiples of 3 up to <math>n 
</math> and <math>B </math> the multiples of 5 up to <math>n </math>, the problem can be reduced to summing the multiples of 3, adding the sum of the multiples of 5, and subtracting the sum of the multiples of 15. For an arbitrarily selected <math>k 
</math>, one can compute the multiples of <math>k </math> up to <math>n </math> via

<math>k + 2k + 3k + \ldots + \lfloor n/k \rfloor k = k (1 + 2 + 3 + \ldots + \lfloor n/k \rfloor) = k \frac{\lfloor n/k \rfloor(\lfloor n/k \rfloor+1)}2</math>

Later problems progress (non-linearly) in difficulty, requiring more creative methodology and higher understanding of the mathematical principles behind the problems.
